summary: Proposes a revised model of who may sign what in DNSSEC, aiming to clarify earlier documents and add restrictions that make secure resolution simpler. In particular it affects which keys are allowed to sign which sets of records. It was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

eli5.summary: In a school, only certain teachers should be allowed to sign certain forms. This clarified who may sign which parts of the Internet's address book. Newer rules later replaced it.

questions: which keys can sign dns records
what are zone keys in dnssec
subtitle: A tighter rule for which DNSSEC keys count as authorized to sign DNS data.

tldr.problem: Early DNSSEC allowed host and user keys, not just zone keys, to produce signatures that resolvers had to treat as valid, which complicated deciding whether a key had authority.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3008 sets field-by-field requirements for a SIG record and its signing KEY record. The main change is that in a secure zone, zone data must be signed by the zone key.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035 and updated by RFC 3658, so the later DNSSEC documents now define signing authority.

today: RFC 3008 was a Proposed Standard that updated RFC 2535. It is obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, and was updated by RFC 3658.

sections.title: What the RFC Changes
sections.content:
RFC 3008 adds restrictions on DNSSEC SIG records, which carry signatures, relating to their authority to sign data. It sets a standard policy for a secure resolver, which local rules can augment. It builds on RFC 2535 and updates section 2.3.6 of that document.

The most significant change is that in a secure zone, zone data is required to be signed by the zone key.
sections.eli5: The old rule let many kinds of people sign the forms. The new rule says only the zone's official signer counts.

sections.title: Checking the SIG Record
sections.content:
A SIG usually covers an RRset, proving its authenticity and integrity. It may also be a SIG(0) with a type covered of 0, attached to a message to protect its integrity. A SIG that is relevant to validation is called material; others are immaterial, and once a SIG is shown to be immaterial no further validation is needed.

Field requirements, all of which MUST be met:

  • Type covered matches the RRset type, or is 0 for SIG(0).
  • The algorithm is recognized by the client and has a defined SIG format.
  • The labels count is no more than the number of labels in the owner name.
  • The original TTL is greater than or equal to the SIG's own TTL.
  • The current time lies between inception and expiration.
  • The signer's name is the zone the data belongs to, and signer name, key tag and algorithm together identify a zone key.

There are no restrictions on the key tag or signature fields.
sections.eli5: Before trusting a signed note, you check the date, the signer's name and the kind of seal. If any check fails, you ignore the note.

sections.title: Checking the Signing KEY
sections.content:
The resolver looks for a KEY matching the signer name, key tag and algorithm. If none is found, the SIG cannot be verified and is immaterial. If several match, all are checked, because only verification shows which one signed.

The KEY must have a flags value of 00 or 01, meaning authentication is allowed, and a protocol value of 3 (DNSSEC) or 255 (ALL). Its algorithm must equal the SIG's. For a data SIG, the KEY name type MUST be 01 (zone), and a resolver MUST ignore non-zone keys unless local policy says otherwise. For a SIG(0), the key SHOULD be a user (00) or host (10) key, since transactions are started by hosts or users, not zones.
sections.eli5: The stamp must be one that is allowed for signing, and for official papers it must be the zone's own stamp, not a visitor's.

sections.title: Why Only Zone Keys
sections.content:
RFC 2535 allowed host and user keys to make material signatures mainly so dynamic update would not need online zone keys. The RFC says that goal cannot be achieved, because online zone keys are needed to sign NXT and SOA sets anyway. With the goal gone, so is the reason for host and user signatures.

Limiting material signatures to zone keys makes the verification chain length bounded by the name's label depth, and a key's authority is clearly defined. No flexibility is lost, as hosts and users can still authenticate update requests to the primary zone server.
sections.eli5: Since the school office has to keep its own stamp handy anyway, there is no need to let everyone have a stamp.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines a baseline for a DNSSEC capable resolver, which a thorough security analysis of DNSSEC needs. By adding restrictions that a signature must pass before it earns DNSSEC trust, it aims to simplify the protocol and make it more robust under scrutiny by the security community.
sections.eli5: Simpler rules are harder to trick, so a clear checklist makes the system safer.
